title: Writing scripts that fail safely
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write a script that stops when something goes wrong instead of carrying on and doing damage — the difference between automation you can trust and automation that scales your mistakes.

blocks.text: Automation multiplies whatever you gave it. A careful command run by hand affects one thing; the same command in a script that runs nightly affects everything, every night, with nobody watching. This lesson is the set of habits that make that safe.
The three-word line that prevents most disasters

blocks.caption: Put this under the shebang
lines: # -e  stop immediately if any command fails
# -u  treat an unset variable as an error instead of an empty string
# -o pipefail  a pipeline fails if ANY stage fails, not just the last one

blocks.title: What each flag actually saves you from
blocks.text: Without -e, a failed cd is ignored and the next line runs in the wrong directory. Without -u, a typo in a variable name expands to nothing — so rm -rf "$BACKUP_DIR/old" becomes rm -rf "/old" when the name was misspelt. Without pipefail, a pipeline reports success because the final tee worked, even though the command feeding it failed.

rows: Refuses to run when dir is empty instead of erasing /
A failed cd no longer leaves you elsewhere
A scheduler has a different PATH than your shell
-- stops a filename starting with - being read as a flag
Spaces in names no longer split into extra arguments

blocks.title: ${var:?message} is the cheapest safety net there is
blocks.text: It expands to the value if set, and exits with your message if not. One extra line in a destructive script converts a silent catastrophe into a clear refusal.
Clean up after yourself, even when it fails

blocks.caption: trap runs on the way out
lines: # whether the script succeeds, fails, or is interrupted,

blocks.text: mktemp -d creates a uniquely named temporary directory instead of a predictable one, which also closes a small security hole: a predictable name in /tmp can be created in advance by someone else, since /tmp is world-writable.
Show what you would do before you do it

blocks.caption: A dry-run switch costs four lines

blocks.text: Now the same script can be read out loud before it is trusted. On anything destructive, being able to run it in a mode that only prints is worth far more than the four lines it costs.

blocks.title: Check your script before running it
blocks.text: shellcheck is a linter for shell scripts and it is very good. It catches unquoted variables, unreachable code, and the classic mistakes before they run. Install it and run shellcheck yourscript.sh — treat what it says as a review, not a nuisance.

blocks.title: Watch the safety flags work
steps: Create unsafe.sh:  #!/bin/bash then:  cd /nonexistent   then:  echo "still running in $(pwd)"
Run it — note that it prints a line even though cd failed
Add set -euo pipefail under the shebang and run it again — now it stops
Create a script with:  echo "deleting ${TARGET}/old"  and run it without setting TARGET
Add set -u and run again — it now refuses instead of expanding to /old
Run: shellcheck unsafe.sh    (if installed — read every warning)
blocks.expected: The same script continuing dangerously, then refusing to. The second case is the important one: an unset variable turning a path into / is exactly how a cleanup script erases a system.

cheatsheet: set -euo pipefail on line two of every script you will run unattended
-e stop on failure · -u unset variable is an error · pipefail any stage failing fails the pipeline
${var:?message} refuses to run when the value is missing
cd "$dir" || exit 1 — never continue after a failed cd
Use absolute paths in anything a scheduler runs
rm -- *.tmp so a leading dash is not read as a flag
mktemp -d for temporary space · trap 'cleanup' EXIT to remove it
Add a --dry-run mode to anything destructive
shellcheck script.sh finds these mistakes before they run

checkpoint.prompt: What does set -u protect you from?

choices.A: Files with spaces in their names
choices.B: An unset variable expanding to nothing
choices.C: Running the script as the wrong user entirely

checkpoint.explanation: Which can turn "$DIR/old" into "/old". By default the shell expands an unset variable to an empty string and carries on. -u makes that an error, which is what you want in anything that deletes or moves data.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a scheduled script need absolute paths?

choices.A: Relative paths are never allowed in shell scripts
choices.B: Absolute paths are faster to resolve
choices.C: A scheduler runs with a smaller PATH and cwd

checkpoint.explanation: This is the classic 'works when I run it, fails on schedule' cause: the command was found in your PATH but not in the scheduler's. Usually much smaller, and with a different working directory than your interactive shell.

choices.A: Removes the temp dir when the script exits
choices.B: It deletes the directory immediately on creation
choices.C: It prevents the script from exiting
choices.D: It traps errors and ignores them

checkpoint.explanation: Whether it succeeded, failed, or was interrupted. Cleanup that only runs on the success path is cleanup that never runs on the day it matters. trap ... EXIT covers every way out.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the value of a --dry-run mode in a destructive script?

choices.A: It makes the script run faster
choices.B: Prints what it would do, without doing it
choices.C: It restricts the script to non-root users
choices.D: It automatically backs up files first

checkpoint.explanation: The plan can be reviewed before it is trusted. It turns an irreversible action into a reviewable one, which is the cheapest safety measure available for automation.
